# Temporal dynamics of inquiry

If intelligence is to be located in process rather than in some occult disposition of a substrate, the temporal grain at which one observes that process becomes a constitutive question rather than a methodological convenience (Thelen & Smith, 1994). What is striking here is that much of the apparatus inherited from cognitive psychology — single-trial response times, accuracy at fixed deadlines, the partitioning of behaviour into discrete responses to discrete stimuli — assumes precisely what a process account of inquiry has to put into question: that the relevant unit of behaviour is short, bounded, and decomposable from the activity that surrounds it (Newell, 1990).

The temporally extended structure of real inquiry — its return to earlier framings, its readiness to abandon a productive line because a more promising one has surfaced, its tendency to make sense of an episode retrospectively in light of what came later — has been documented for decades in studies of skilled practice and scientific reasoning, yet has rarely been incorporated into operational definitions of the cognitive abilities that putatively underwrite such activity (Schön, 1983). What is striking here is that the practitioners who furnish the data for such studies almost universally describe their own competence in terms of dispositions to act over time, not in terms of momentary capacities — a description the prevailing psychometric paradigm has no straightforward way to honour.

A process account need not deny that there are short-timescale phenomena worth measuring; the point is rather that one cannot read a theory of intelligence directly off the short-timescale measure without an argument linking the two — an argument that the differential-psychology tradition has tended to assume rather than to discharge (Sternberg, 1985). Notably, the failure of standard cognitive-ability measures to predict performance in temporally extended professional and scholarly settings is not a marginal anomaly. It is the predictable consequence of measuring at one grain and theorizing about another.

The chapters that follow take this scale-mismatch as their starting point, and develop the constructive proposal that intelligence — to the extent the term picks out something worth keeping — names a way of being organized in time, not a quantity of cognitive substance (Clark, 1997).
